label: Book I
title: What I Owe
paragraphs: From my grandfather Verus: a good nature, and freedom from anger.
2. From my father's reputation, and from my memory of him: modesty, and a manly character.

3. From my mother: reverence for the gods; generosity; the habit of refusing not only to do wrong but even to entertain the thought of it; and beyond that, plainness in the way I live, far from the style of the rich.
4. From my great-grandfather: not being sent to the public schools; having good teachers at home instead; and learning that on things like these, you should spend without counting.

5. From the man who raised me: to back neither the Greens nor the Blues at the races, and neither the short shields nor the long at the gladiators' fights; to carry hard work, and need little; to do my own work with my own hands; to keep out of other people's business; and to be slow to believe a slander.

6. From Diognetus: not to pour myself into empty enthusiasms; to put no faith in what the wonder-workers and conjurers say about incantations, or the driving out of spirits, and all the rest of it; not to raise quails for the fights, and not to lose my head over sports like that; to put up with frank talk; to have made myself at home in philosophy — hearing Bacchius first, then Tandasis and Marcianus; to have written dialogues as a boy; and to have wanted the hard cot and the animal skin and everything else that goes with the Greek training.

7. From Rusticus: the first suspicion that my character needed correcting — needed tending; and not to be pulled aside into the sophist's game: writing tracts on theory, delivering tidy little sermons, striking the pose of the ascetic or the benefactor for effect. To stay away from rhetoric, from poetry, from elegant phrasing; not to stroll around the house in ceremonial dress, or do anything else of the kind; to write letters simply, like the one he himself wrote to my mother from Sinuessa. To be easy to call back, easy to reconcile, when someone has lost his temper with me or done me wrong — the moment he is willing to return. To read exactly, and not to be satisfied with the general drift of a book; not to nod along too fast with the ones who talk in circles. And to have come to know the recorded talks of Epictetus, which he shared with me from his own library.

[Editor's note: Marcus's phrase is 'the hypomnemata of Epictetus' — his notes, his recorded talks. It should not be translated 'the writings of Epictetus,' because Epictetus wrote nothing. His student Arrian, who preserved for us everything we know of Epictetus, said of his own transcripts: 'These notes I tried to keep for myself, to save a record of his thinking' (Letter to Gellius).]

8. From Apollonius: independence of mind, and a steadiness of purpose the dice of fortune cannot touch; to look to nothing else, not even for a moment, except reason; to stay the same man through stabbing pain, the loss of a child, long illness; to see plainly, in a living example, that the same man can be all intensity and all ease; to explain without impatience; to have had before my eyes a man who plainly counted his experience, and his skill at opening up philosophy, the least of his gifts; and to have learned how to accept from friends what pass for favors — neither surrendering to them nor letting them go by unfelt.

9. From Sextus: kindliness; the picture of a household governed by a father; the idea of living according to nature; dignity with no acting in it; an intuition for what friends needed, and a guardian's care in meeting it; patience with the untrained, and with people whose opinions arrive before their thinking. He fit himself to everyone: talking with him was more winning than any flattery, and yet in that same hour the people he charmed held him in the deepest respect. He had a sure, methodical way of finding and ordering the principles a life cannot do without. He never showed so much as the surface of anger, or of any other passion: he was the most passionless of men, and the most affectionate. He could praise without applause in his voice, and he wore great learning without showing it off.

10. From Alexander the grammarian: not to be a fault-finder; when someone comes out with a barbarism, a solecism, or a phrase that grates on the ear, not to pounce with a rebuke, but to bring out, deftly, the very expression that should have been used — folded into an answer, or a seconding of the point, or a joint look at the thing itself (the thing, not the word), or some other graceful, glancing reminder.
11. From Fronto: to see what envy, duplicity, and hypocrisy look like in a tyrant; and that the men we call patricians are somehow rather short on natural affection.

12. From Alexander the Platonist: not to say to anyone — or write in a letter — 'I have no time,' not often, and never without real necessity; and not to use the press of business as a standing excuse for sliding out of the duties we owe the people we live with.

13. From Catulus: not to wave off a friend's complaint, even an unfair one, but to try to restore things to their old footing; to speak of teachers warmly and gratefully, as is remembered of Domitius and Athenodotus; and to love my children truly.

14. From Severus: love of family, love of truth, love of justice; to have come, through him, to know Thrasea, Helvidius, Cato, Dion, Brutus; to have conceived the idea of a commonwealth of equal law, governed by equality and equal freedom of speech, and of a monarchy that honors, above everything, the liberty of the governed. From him too: an even, unslackening respect for philosophy; doing good, and giving open-handedly; hopefulness; and trust that my friends love me. He was open with anyone he condemned, and his friends never had to guess at what he wanted or didn't want: it was plain.

15. From Maximus: self-command, and a mind nothing could spin off course; good cheer in every circumstance, sickness included; a character mixed just right — gentle, and grave; doing the work in front of him without complaint. Everyone believed that he spoke as he thought, and that whatever he did, he did without a single bad intention. Nothing amazed him; nothing rattled him. He was never rushed, never dragging, never at a loss, never dejected, never wearing a pasted-on smile — and never, on the other side, angry or suspicious. He was generous, quick to forgive, and honest; he gave you the impression of a man who could not be bent rather than one who is kept straight. No one ever felt condescended to by him, and no one ever dared to think himself the better man. And he had a gift for humor that charmed.

16. In my father I watched gentleness — and an immovable grip on decisions he had examined and made; no vanity about so-called honors; a love of work, and stamina; an open ear for anyone with something to offer the common good; the undeviating habit of giving each man what he deserved; and a sure feel for when to bear down and when to let up. He put an end to the affairs with boys. He thought of himself as a citizen like any other: his friends were under no obligation to dine with him or to appear at his side when he traveled, and whoever stayed behind on some errand of their own found him unchanged toward them. In council he questioned closely and he kept at it; he never broke off the search early, satisfied with whatever lay on the surface. He held on to his friends — never tiring of them, never doting either. Sufficient in everything, and sunny. He looked far down the road and arranged the smallest things in advance, without a scene. Cheering and flattery of every kind stopped in front of him. He kept constant watch on what the empire actually needed, stewarded its treasury, and stood the criticism this earned him. Toward the gods, no superstition; toward men, no pandering, no crowd-pleasing, no courting the mob — sober everywhere, steady, never tasteless, never chasing novelty. The comforts that make life easier — and fortune poured those out for him — he used without swagger and without apology: when they were there, he enjoyed them frankly; when they were not, he did not miss them. No one could say of him 'a sophist,' 'a smart-mouthed house slave,' 'a pedant.' What they said was: a ripe man, a complete one, above flattery, fit to manage his own affairs and other people's. Beyond all this, he honored genuine philosophers, and the other kind he neither insulted nor followed. He was easy in conversation, agreeable without laying it on. He took sensible care of his own body — not like a man greedy for life, not for looks, and not carelessly either — so that by his own attention he almost never needed doctors, drugs, or salves. Above all, he stepped aside, without a flicker of envy, for anyone with a real ability — for speaking, for law, for custom, for anything else — and pushed alongside them, so that each might come into the honor his own strength deserved. He did everything in the manner of his ancestors, and did not perform even that — the keeping of the old ways — for anyone's notice. He was not restless, not a man who shifts from thing to thing: he liked the same places and the same occupations, and after each siege of headache he came back fresh, at full strength, to the usual work. His secrets were few — very few, very rare, and only ever about matters of state. He showed sense and measure in staging the spectacles, in public works, in handouts of money to the people and things of that kind: the acts of a man with his eye on what needed doing, not on the reputation for having done it. He did not bathe at odd hours; he was not forever building houses; he gave no thought to fancy eating, to the weave and color of his clothes, to the beauty of his slaves. His dress came up from Lorium, from the villa on the coast; from Lanuvium, most of the rest. The way he treated the toll collector at Tusculum, who came asking his pardon — that was his whole way of dealing with the world. Nothing in him was harsh, or implacable, or driving; nothing ever taken, as they say, 'to the sweating point'; everything was thought out piece by piece, as if he had all the time in the world — unhurried, in order, with strength, each part agreeing with the rest. What is remembered of Socrates would fit him exactly: he could abstain from, and he could enjoy, the things most people are too weak to abstain from and too indulgent to enjoy. To be strong in the one and clear-headed in the other is the mark of a man with a finished, unconquerable soul — the soul he showed in Maximus's illness.

17. To the gods I owe this: good grandfathers, good parents, a good sister, good teachers, a good household — good relatives, good friends, good nearly everything; and that I never blundered into wronging any of them, though there was that in my temperament which, given the opening, might well have done it. It was the gods' kindness that no combination of circumstances ever arose to expose me. That I was not raised longer than I was in the keeping of my grandfather's concubine; that I kept the bloom of my youth, and did not rush to prove my manhood before its season, but held off even a little past it. That I was placed under a ruler and a father who was going to strip me of every scrap of vanity, and bring me to understand that a man can live in a palace and need no bodyguards, no embroidered robes, no torch-bearers and statues and the rest of that pomp — that he can pull his life in almost to a private citizen's compass, and lose for it nothing in dignity and nothing in force when the common good requires a ruler's hand. That I was given a brother whose character could rouse me to keep watch over myself, and whose respect and affection warmed me. That my children were not born dull or twisted in body. That I got no further than I did in rhetoric, in poetry, in the other studies that might have held me for good if I had felt myself making smooth progress. That I moved quickly to give the people who raised me the standing they seemed to want, and did not put them off with the excuse that, since they were still young, I would see to it later. That I knew Apollonius, Rusticus, Maximus. That the picture of what a life according to nature is came to me clearly, and came often — so that, as far as the gods are concerned, with their gifts and their help and their promptings, nothing has kept me from living according to nature this long while; if I still fall short of it, that is my own fault: I have not kept the reminders — the near-instructions — that the gods keep sending. That my body has held out this long, in a life like this one. That I never touched Benedicta or Theodotus, and that later, when the passions of love did catch me, I came out whole. That, angry as I often was at Rusticus, I never went beyond anger to the thing I would have regretted. That my mother, though fated to die young, still spent her last years with me. That every time I wanted to help someone poor or otherwise in need, I never once heard that there was no money for it; and that I never fell into such need myself as to have to take from another. That my wife is who she is: so obedient, so loving, so unaffected. That there was no shortage of good teachers for my children. That remedies were shown to me in dreams — against the spitting of blood, against dizziness, among others. And that when the hunger for philosophy took me, I did not fall into the hands of some sophist, did not settle down to picking apart texts or syllogisms, and did not lose myself in the study of the skies. For all these things need the gods' help — and fortune's.
Among the Quadi, on the River Granua.

[Editor's note: If these words are genuine, Marcus may have written this first book during the campaign against the Quadi. In the first printed edition of the Meditations, and in the older editions that followed, the first three sections of Book II stood at the end of Book I; Gataker moved them to the head of Book II.]

divergences.older: good morals and the government of my temper
divergences.lectio: a good nature, and freedom from anger
divergences.note: ἀόργητον names the absence of anger, not its management. Long's 'government of my temper' turns a settled state into an ongoing struggle; the Stoic claim — and the ledger's — is that in Verus the anger simply was not there.

divergences.lectio: somehow rather short on natural affection
divergences.note: στοργή is family affection broadly, not fatherly feeling in particular; 'paternal' narrows Fronto's barb about the whole patrician class. And πως — 'somehow' — carries a shrug worth keeping.

The Greek of this edition has no 'brother.' Severus is almost certainly Claudius Severus the Peripatetic — Marcus's friend and later his daughter's father-in-law, not his brother — so I follow the Greek and drop Long's gloss rather than bake in a genealogy the text does not assert.

translatorNote: The hardest call was the ledger form itself: the Greek of Book I has almost no main verbs — just 'From X: the such-and-such' — so I kept the colon-ledger and let 'I learned' stay implicit, opening into full sentences only where Marcus himself does (Sextus, Maximus, his father). In I.8 I restored the gambling metaphor buried in ἀκύβευτον — 'a steadiness of purpose the dice of fortune cannot touch' — where Long flattens it to 'undeviating steadiness.' I deliberately did not soften the wife's πειθήνιον ('so obedient'): it is what Marcus wrote, and it is evidence about him and his world. Where the text is corrupt — the dream-oracle at Caieta in I.17 — I follow Long in passing over it silently rather than printing a guess. Long's two editorial notes and the Granua subscription are kept in place, recast as modern editor's notes, so the paragraphs align one-for-one with his edition.
